src_text: When it comes to those who have waded into that kind of deep water, some have tried the Let's-really-shake-things-up solution. There's the lamentable 1962 remake of "The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari," for instance, which not only eliminated the central figure of Cesare the somnambulist but also featured a Caligari who instead of practicing diabolic hypnotism spent his time showing the heroine offensive pictures. Other filmmakers have chosen the even more baffling route of changing almost nothing, such as Gus Van Sant's nearly shot-for-shot 1998 remake of "Psycho." The number of disappointed moviegoers you risk in remaking a masterpiece from 1922 is smaller, for obvious reasons, but even so, the director Robert Eggers has made clear in any number of interviews his understanding that his new "Nosferatu" is re-engaging one of the greatest of the silent movies. (In 2016, when he was first attempting to remake the film, he told an interviewer that it felt "ugly and blasphemous and egomaniacal and disgusting" to take up that project so early into his career.)
target_text: Что касается тех, кто затеял подобные глубоководные погружения, некоторые из них попытались применить радикальное решение. Например, есть жалкий ремейк «Кабинета доктора Калигари» 1962 года, в котором не только убрали центрального персонажа — сомнамбулу Чезаре, но и изобразили Калигари, который вместо того, чтобы заниматься дьявольским гипнотизмом, проводил время, показывая героине оскорбительные картинки. Другие режиссеры выбрали еще более непонятный путь — почти ничего не менять, как, например, в почти кадр в кадр повторяющемся ремейке «Психо» 1998 года, снятом Гасом Ван Сэнтом. Количество разочарованных зрителей, которых вы рискуете получить, пере снимая шедевр 1922 года, по понятным причинам меньше, но, тем не менее, режиссер Роберт Эггерс в многочисленных интервью ясно дал понять, что понимает, что его новый «Носферату» — это возрождение одного из величайших немых фильмов. (В 2016 году, когда он впервые попытался переснять фильм, он сказал интервьюеру, что ему казалось «уродливым, кощунственным, эгоистичным и отвратительным» браться за этот проект так рано в своей карьере.)

src_text: But the most destabilizing figure might well be Hutter's wife, Ellen, our heroine, who's again and again shown to be telepathically on the monster's wavelength, even when he's thousands of miles away, so that polarities like good and evil or desire and repulsion seem to just evaporate while we watch. That last aspect alone would seem to land this story in Robert Eggers's wheelhouse. Part of the subversive energy of movies like "The Witch," "The Lighthouse" and "The Northman" derives from what feels like modern takes on historical characters in thrall to dark passions so that the distantly historical is both granted its strangeness and animated by a scrutinizing modern sensibility. At its best, his version both evokes and reconceives Murnau's most brilliant visual ideas. Murnau's masterful use of the opacities of dark archways from which the vampire can emerge and into which he can dissolve is both echoed and made new. Murnau's famously arresting use of shadows to visualize the vampire's defiling reach is reimagined when those shadows in this new version extend themselves in a 360-degree pan that evokes their vertiginous inescapability. And the shadow of the vampire's hand now extends across the entire city, repurposing the most memorable image from Murnau's "Faust."
target_text: Но самой дестабилизирующей фигурой, возможно, является жена Хаттера, Эллен, наша героиня, которая снова и снова демонстрирует, что телепатически находится на одной волне с монстром, даже когда он находится за тысячи миль от нее, так что полярности, такие как добро и зло или желание и отвращение, кажутся просто испаряющимися на наших глазах. Только этот последний аспект, казалось бы, помещает эту историю в сферу интересов Роберта Эггерса. Часть подрывной энергии фильмов вроде «Ведьмы», «Маяк» и «Нормандия» проистекает из того, что кажется современным взглядом на исторических персонажей, порабощенных темными страстями, так что отдаленно историческое одновременно обретает свою странность и оживляется современным анализирующим восприятием. В лучшем своем проявлении его версия как вызывает, так и заново представляет самые блестящие визуальные идеи Мурнау. Мастерское использование Мурнау непрозрачности темных аркад, из которых может появиться вампир и в которые он может раствориться, как отражается, так и становится новым. Знаменитое захватывающее использование теней Мурнау для визуализации оскверняющего влияния вампира переосмысливается, когда эти тени в этой новой версии распространяются в панораме на 360 градусов, что вызывает ощущение их головокружительной неизбежности. src_text: South African opener Matthew Breetzke etched his name into the record books by becoming the first batter to score 150 runs on ODI debut in second match of the ongoing tri-series against New Zealand at the Gaddafi Stadium on Monday. His stunning knock of 150 off 148 balls, laced with 11 fours and five sixes, surpassed the previous record held by the legendary West Indies' batter Desmond Haynes, who scored 148 in his maiden ODI innings against Australia back in 1978. Before Breetzke's innings, the highest score on ODI debut for South Africa was 124 by Colin Ingram against Zimbabwe in 2010. Now, Breetzke stands alone at the top, delivering a performance that showcased patience, aggression, and remarkable shot selection as South Africa posted a mammoth 304/6.
target_text: L'apertura sudafricano Matthew Breetzke ha scritto il suo nome nei libri dei record diventando il primo battitore a segnare 150 run al debutto in ODI nella seconda partita del tri-series in corso contro la Nuova Zelanda allo Gaddafi Stadium lunedì. Il suo straordinario innings di 150 run in 148 palline, arricchito da 11 quattro e cinque sei, ha superato il precedente record detenuto dalla leggenda delle Indie Occidentali Desmond Haynes, che aveva segnato 148 nel suo primo innings ODI contro l'Australia nel 1978. src_text: F. W. Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.
target_text: Фильм Ф. В. Мурнау "Носферату: Симфония ужаса" сам по себе является ремейком – неавторизованной адаптацией "Дракулы", непреодолимо увлекательного призрачного романа Брема Стокера – и Мурнау и сценарист Хенрик Галеен сохранили многое из того, что было поразительным в оригинале, внося при этом крупные изменения: они, например, заложили основу теперь уже устоявшейся традиции, по которой солнечный свет может уничтожить вампира, что ни разу не упоминалось в книге Стокера. Вероятно, я смотрел "Носферату" в слишком юном возрасте. Мне было 6 лет, PBS показывало такие вещи, а моя няня просто радовалась, что я не поджигаю дом. Но он произвел на меня невероятное впечатление в любой из моих сеансов просмотра. Это было похоже на ощущение сквозняка из могилы. (Эффект был настолько продолжительным, что 30 лет спустя я опубликовал роман, вдохновленный фильмом и его производством.) src_text: F. W. Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.

src_text: F. W. Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.

src_text: I've always thought that one of the most insoluble aesthetic problems going is remaking a movie masterpiece. I certainly understand the impulse to passionately re-engage such a work, but if the definition of a masterwork is something peerless at what it sought to accomplish, how do you remake it without simply reiterating it? There's a reason no one has tried second versions of Fellini's "8½" or Coppola's "The Godfather" or Polanski's "Chinatown." In the case of Fellini's achievement, is someone going to produce a more harrowing portrait of the self-deluding toxicity of male narcissism? In the case of Coppola's, of the corrosive effects of power? Or in the case of Polanski's, of the Hey-nothing-personal malevolence of late-model capitalism? (Water itself in that movie turns out to be the commodity that's manipulated for profit.)

src_text: When it comes to those who have waded into that kind of deep water, some have tried the Let's-really-shake-things-up solution. There's the lamentable 1962 remake of "The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari," for instance, which not only eliminated the central figure of Cesare the somnambulist but also featured a Caligari who instead of practicing diabolic hypnotism spent his time showing the heroine offensive pictures. Other filmmakers have chosen the even more baffling route of changing almost nothing, such as Gus Van Sant's nearly shot-for-shot 1998 remake of "Psycho." The number of disappointed moviegoers you risk in remaking a masterpiece from 1922 is smaller, for obvious reasons, but even so, the director Robert Eggers has made clear in any number of interviews his understanding that his new "Nosferatu" is re-engaging one of the greatest of the silent movies. (In 2016, when he was first attempting to remake the film, he told an interviewer that it felt "ugly and blasphemous and egomaniacal and disgusting" to take up that project so early into his career.)

His stunning knock of 150 off 148 balls, laced with 11 fours and five sixes, surpassed the previous record held by the legendary West Indies' batter Desmond Haynes, who scored 148 in his maiden ODI innings against Australia back in 1978. Before Breetzke's innings, the highest score on ODI debut for South Africa was 124 by Colin Ingram against Zimbabwe in 2010. Now, Breetzke stands alone at the top, delivering a performance that showcased patience, aggression, and remarkable shot selection as South Africa posted a mammoth 304/6.
target_text: Durante la seconda partita della tri-serie in corso contro la Nuova Zelanda al Gaddafi Stadium, lunedì, l'opener sudafricano Matthew Breetzke ha scritto il suo nome nei libri dei record diventando il primo battitore a segnare 150 punti nel suo debutto in ODI. La sua impressionante battuta, di 150 punti su un totale di 148 palle, con 11 quattro e cinque sei, ha superato il precedente record detenuto dal leggendario battitore delle Indie Occidentali, Desmond Haynes, che ne aveva segnati 148 nella sua prima inning in ODI contro l'Australia nel 1978. Prima dell'inning di Breetzke, il punteggio più alto in un debutto in ODI per il Sudafrica era di 124 punti, segnati da Colin Ingram contro lo Zimbabwe nel 2010. Ora, Breetzke è da solo in cima alla classifica, con una performance che ha mostrato pazienza, aggressività e una notevole selezione di colpi, mentre il Sudafrica ha segnato un mammut 304/6.

src_text: F. W. Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.

src_text: F. W. Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.
target_text: "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" eftir F. W. Murnau er sjálft endurgerð - óleyfisbundið aðlögun "Dracula", þess leiðandi lesilega draugadraums Bram Stoker - og Murnau og handritshöfundurinn Henrik Galeen héldu mikið af því sem var hrífandi við upprunalegu meðan þeir settu inn eigin stórar breytingar: Þeir bera til dæmis ábyrgð á nú fastmótaðri hefðinni að sólarljós geti eyðilagt vampírann, hugmynd sem finnst hvergi í bók Stoker. Ég sá líklega "Nosferatu" á of viðkvæmum aldri. Ég var 6 ára, PBS var að sýna slíkar myndir og barnapíuna mína var einfaldlega ánægju að ég var ekki að brenna húsið niður. En ég hefði verið flattur af henni hvenær sem ég hefði séð hana. Það var eins og að hafa fundið fyrir drögum frá gröf. (Áhrifin voru svo langvarandi að 30 eða fleiri árum síðar gaf ég út skáldsögu innblásna af myndinni og framleiðslu hennar.) Allt saman var ekki svo skelfilegt sem frekar ógnvænlegt, og allt byrjaði með sjálfan Nosferatu. Leikur Max Schreck er, 102 árum síðar, enn viðmiðið fyrir ógnvænlegt og virtur viðbjóð. Vampírinn Schreck hefur kyrrstöðu eins og persóna í martröð eða kónguló á vef hennar, og heimurinn sem hann býr í er stundum jafn ógnvænlegur. Eftir fyrsta skelfilega nóttina í kastala Nosferatu, tekur Hutter, hetjan okkar, eftir í speglinum að eitthvað hefur bitið háls hans, og brosir.

src_text: But the most destabilizing figure might well be Hutter's wife, Ellen, our heroine, who's again and again shown to be telepathically on the monster's wavelength, even when he's thousands of miles away, so that polarities like good and evil or desire and repulsion seem to just evaporate while we watch. That last aspect alone would seem to land this story in Robert Eggers's wheelhouse. Part of the subversive energy of movies like "The Witch," "The Lighthouse" and "The Northman" derives from what feels like modern takes on historical characters in thrall to dark passions so that the distantly historical is both granted its strangeness and animated by a scrutinizing modern sensibility. At its best, his version both evokes and reconceives Murnau's most brilliant visual ideas. Murnau's masterful use of the opacities of dark archways from which the vampire can emerge and into which he can dissolve is both echoed and made new. Murnau's famously arresting use of shadows to visualize the vampire's defiling reach is reimagined when those shadows in this new version extend themselves in a 360-degree pan that evokes their vertiginous inescapability. And the shadow of the vampire's hand now extends across the entire city, repurposing the most memorable image from Murnau's "Faust."

Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.

src_text: When it comes to those who have waded into that kind of deep water, some have tried the Let's-really-shake-things-up solution. There's the lamentable 1962 remake of "The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari," for instance, which not only eliminated the central figure of Cesare the somnambulist but also featured a Caligari who instead of practicing diabolic hypnotism spent his time showing the heroine offensive pictures. Other filmmakers have chosen the even more baffling route of changing almost nothing, such as Gus Van Sant's nearly shot-for-shot 1998 remake of "Psycho." The number of disappointed moviegoers you risk in remaking a masterpiece from 1922 is smaller, for obvious reasons, but even so, the director Robert Eggers has made clear in any number of interviews his understanding that his new "Nosferatu" is re-engaging one of the greatest of the silent movies. (In 2016, when he was first attempting to remake the film, he told an interviewer that it felt "ugly and blasphemous and egomaniacal and disgusting" to take up that project so early into his career.)

src_text: South African opener Matthew Breetzke etched his name into the record books by becoming the first batter to score 150 runs on ODI debut in second match of the ongoing tri-series against New Zealand at the Gaddafi Stadium on Monday. His stunning knock of 150 off 148 balls, laced with 11 fours and five sixes, surpassed the previous record held by the legendary West Indies' batter Desmond Haynes, who scored 148 in his maiden ODI innings against Australia back in 1978. Before Breetzke's innings, the highest score on ODI debut for South Africa was 124 by Colin Ingram against Zimbabwe in 2010. Now, Breetzke stands alone at the top, delivering a performance that showcased patience, aggression, and remarkable shot selection as South Africa posted a mammoth 304/6.

La sua straordinaria prestazione di 150 run su 148 palle, arricchita da 11 boundary e cinque six, ha superato il precedente record detenuto dal leggendario battitore delle West Indies Desmond Haynes, che segnò 148 run nel suo primo innings ODI contro l'Australia nel 1978. Prima dell'innings di Breetzke, il punteggio più alto in un debutto ODI per il Sudafrica era di 124 run, realizzato da Colin Ingram contro lo Zimbabwe nel 2010. Ora, Breetzke domina in solitaria, con una performance che ha dimostrato pazienza, aggressività e una notevole selezione dei colpi, mentre il Sudafrica ha totalizzato un mastodontico 304/6.

src_text: But the most destabilizing figure might well be Hutter's wife, Ellen, our heroine, who's again and again shown to be telepathically on the monster's wavelength, even when he's thousands of miles away, so that polarities like good and evil or desire and repulsion seem to just evaporate while we watch. That last aspect alone would seem to land this story in Robert Eggers's wheelhouse. Part of the subversive energy of movies like "The Witch," "The Lighthouse" and "The Northman" derives from what feels like modern takes on historical characters in thrall to dark passions so that the distantly historical is both granted its strangeness and animated by a scrutinizing modern sensibility. At its best, his version both evokes and reconceives Murnau's most brilliant visual ideas. Murnau's masterful use of the opacities of dark archways from which the vampire can emerge and into which he can dissolve is both echoed and made new. Murnau's famously arresting use of shadows to visualize the vampire's defiling reach is reimagined when those shadows in this new version extend themselves in a 360-degree pan that evokes their vertiginous inescapability. And the shadow of the vampire's hand now extends across the entire city, repurposing the most memorable image from Murnau's "Faust."
target_text: Ale nejvíce destabilizující postavou by snad mohla být Hutterova manželka Ellen, naše heroina, která se znovu a znovu ukazuje být telepaticky spojená s tím monstrem, dokonce i když je tisíce kilometrů daleko, takže polarity jako dobro a zlo nebo touha a odpor, jakoby před našima očima mizely. Tento poslední aspekt sám o sobě naznačuje, že by se tato filmová adaptace mohla trefit do střediska zájmů Roberta Egreggese. Část podvratné energie filmů jako "Čarodějka", "Maják" a "Severák" pochází z toho, že se jedná o zjevné moderní pojetí historických postav pod vlivem temných vášní, takže si daleko vzdálená historická událost udržuje svou podivnost a zároveň je oživena kritickou moderní perspektivou. Jeho verze přitom v nejlepších případech jak vyvolává, tak i nově přetváří Murnauovy nejgeniálnější vizuální nápady. Murnauovo mistrovské využívání zatemnění v tmavých průchodech, odkud se upír může vynořit a do kterých může zmizet, je zde nejen připomenuto, ale i obnovené. Murnauovo proslulé využití stínů k vizualizaci upířího oskvrňujícího dosahu je znovu promyšlené, když se tyto stíny v této nové verzi rozprostírají v pohledu o 360 stupňů, což evokuje jejich závratnou neuniknutelnost. A stín upíří ruky se nyní šíří po celém městě, což přetváří jeden z nejzapamatovatelnějších obrazů z Murnauova "Fausta".

src_text: F. W. Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.

src_text: F. W. Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.
target_text:
"Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" eftir F. W. Murnau er í raun endurgerð - óheimildarleg breyting á "Dracula" eftir Bram Stoker, þessarar þvingandi lesnar skáldsögu - og Murnau og handritshöfundurinn Henrik Galeen höfðu varðveitt mikið af því sem var áhrifamikið í upprunalegri sögunni, á sama tíma og þeir gerðu stórar breytingar: þeir eru til dæmis ábyrgir fyrir það að sólarljós geti drepið vampíra, hugmynd sem finnst aldrei í Stoker's bók.
Ég sá líklega "Nosferatu" í of viðkvæman aldri. Ég var 6 ára, PBS sýndi slíka hluti og barnvaktarinn minn var einfaldlega glaður að ég brændi ekki niður húsið. En ég hefði verið hræddur af því hvenær sem ég sá það. Það var eins og að finna loftstreymi frá gröf. (Áhrifin voru svo langvarandi að 30 árum síðar gaf ég út skáldsögu sem var innblundin af myndinni og framleiðslunni.) Heildin var ekki svo mikið skræmdandi og frekar óhuggunleg, og allt þetta hófst með persónunni Nosferatu sjálfum. Frammistaðan hjá Max Schreck er, 102 árum síðar, samt sem áður staðsetningarstaðurinn fyrir grimmleika og virðulega óþægileika. Vampíran hjá Schreck hefur stöðugleika persónu í vondum draumi eða spíra á vefnum sínum, og heimurinn sem hann býr í er stundum jafn óhuggunlegur. Eftir fyrstu ógnvekjandi nóttina hjá hetjunum Hutter í Nosferatu's kastalnum sér hann í speglinum að eitthvað hefur bitað í hálsinn á sér, og hann brosir.

src_text: South African opener Matthew Breetzke etched his name into the record books by becoming the first batter to score 150 runs on ODI debut in second match of the ongoing tri-series against New Zealand at the Gaddafi Stadium on Monday. His stunning knock of 150 off 148 balls, laced with 11 fours and five sixes, surpassed the previous record held by the legendary West Indies' batter Desmond Haynes, who scored 148 in his maiden ODI innings against Australia back in 1978. Before Breetzke's innings, the highest score on ODI debut for South Africa was 124 by Colin Ingram against Zimbabwe in 2010. Now, Breetzke stands alone at the top, delivering a performance that showcased patience, aggression, and remarkable shot selection as South Africa posted a mammoth 304/6.

Tema muljetavaldav 150 jooksu 148 pallilt, mis sisaldas 11 neljast ja viis kuut, ületas varasema rekordi, mida hoidis legendaarne Lääne-India mängija Desmond Haynes, kes lõi 148 oma esimeses ODI-mängus Austraalia vastu 1978. aastal. Enne Breetzke'it oli Lõuna-Aafrika kõrgeim ODI-debüüdiskoor 124, mille saavutas Colin Ingram Zimbabwe vastu 2010. aastal. Nüüd seisab Breetzke üksinda tipus, esitades soorituse, mis näitas kannatlikkust, agressiivsust ja silmapaistvat löögivalikut, aidates Lõuna-Aafrikal koguda muljetavaldavad 304/6.

src_text: South African opener Matthew Breetzke etched his name into the record books by becoming the first batter to score 150 runs on ODI debut in second match of the ongoing tri-series against New Zealand at the Gaddafi Stadium on Monday. His stunning knock of 150 off 148 balls, laced with 11 fours and five sixes, surpassed the previous record held by the legendary West Indies' batter Desmond Haynes, who scored 148 in his maiden ODI innings against Australia back in 1978. Before Breetzke's innings, the highest score on ODI debut for South Africa was 124 by Colin Ingram against Zimbabwe in 2010. Now, Breetzke stands alone at the top, delivering a performance that showcased patience, aggression, and remarkable shot selection as South Africa posted a mammoth 304/6.

Grazie alla sua eccezionale prestazione di 150 run segnati in 148 palle, accompagnati da 11 four e 5 sei, ha superato il precedente record detenuto dal leggendario battitore giamaicano Desmond Haynes, che aveva segnato 148 run nella sua prima apparizione in ODI contro l'Australia nel 1978. Prima dell'ottimo punteggio di Breetzke, la miglior prestazione di sempre per il Sudafrica nel debutto di un match di ODI era stata 124, realizzata da Colin Ingram contro lo Zimbabwe nel 2010. Breetzke si è affermato da solo come il nuovo primatista, mostrando pazienza, aggressività e una notevole scelta di battuta, mentre il Sudafrica ha raggiunto il notevole punteggio di 304/6.

Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.

src_text: F. W. Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.

Ma nägin „Nosferatut“ tõenäoliselt liiga mõjutatavas eas. Ma olin 6-aastane, selliseid asju näidati PBS-is ja minu lapsehoidja oli lihtsalt õnnelik, et ma maja maha ei põletanud. See rabas mind jalust iga kord, kui ma seda nägin. See tundus nagu hauast õhkuv tõmbetuul. (Selle mõju kestis nii kaua, et umbes 30 aastat hiljem avaldasin ma filmist ja selle väntamisest inspireeritud romaani.) Kogu see värk oli verdtarretava asemel pigem olemuslikult häiriv ja kõik see sai alguse Nosferatu enda tegelaskujust. src_text: I've always thought that one of the most insoluble aesthetic problems going is remaking a movie masterpiece. I certainly understand the impulse to passionately re-engage such a work, but if the definition of a masterwork is something peerless at what it sought to accomplish, how do you remake it without simply reiterating it? There's a reason no one has tried second versions of Fellini's "8½" or Coppola's "The Godfather" or Polanski's "Chinatown." In the case of Fellini's achievement, is someone going to produce a more harrowing portrait of the self-deluding toxicity of male narcissism? In the case of Coppola's, of the corrosive effects of power? Or in the case of Polanski's, of the Hey-nothing-personal malevolence of late-model capitalism? (Water itself in that movie turns out to be the commodity that's manipulated for profit.)

src_text: F. W. Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. At its best, his version both evokes and reconceives Murnau's most brilliant visual ideas. Murnau's masterful use of the opacities of dark archways from which the vampire can emerge and into which he can dissolve is both echoed and made new. Murnau's famously arresting use of shadows to visualize the vampire's defiling reach is reimagined when those shadows in this new version extend themselves in a 360-degree pan that evokes their vertiginous inescapability. And the shadow of the vampire's hand now extends across the entire city, repurposing the most memorable image from Murnau's "Faust."

src_text: South African opener Matthew Breetzke etched his name into the record books by becoming the first batter to score 150 runs on ODI debut in second match of the ongoing tri-series against New Zealand at the Gaddafi Stadium on Monday. His stunning knock of 150 off 148 balls, laced with 11 fours and five sixes, surpassed the previous record held by the legendary West Indies' batter Desmond Haynes, who scored 148 in his maiden ODI innings against Australia back in 1978. Before Breetzke's innings, the highest score on ODI debut for South Africa was 124 by Colin Ingram against Zimbabwe in 2010. Now, Breetzke stands alone at the top, delivering a performance that showcased patience, aggression, and remarkable shot selection as South Africa posted a mammoth 304/6.
target_text: Jihoafrický pálkař Matthew Breetzke se v pondělí na stadionu Gaddafi zapsal do historických tabulek, když se ve druhém zápase probíhající série tří zemí proti Novému Zélandu stal prvním pálkařem, který při svém debutu v ODI zaznamenal 150 runů. Svým úžasným výkonem 150 runů ze 148 míčků, který zahrnoval 11 čtyřek a pět šestek, překonal předchozí rekord legendárního západoindického pálkaře Desmonda Haynese, jenž v roce 1978 při svém prvním ODI startu proti Austrálii nasbíral 148 runů. Před Breetzkeho výkonem držel jihoafrický rekord v počtu runů při debutu v ODI Colin Ingram se 124 runy proti Zimbabwe z roku 2010. Nyní Breetzke stojí sám na vrcholu díky výkonu, který ukázal trpělivost, agresivitu a pozoruhodný výběr úderů a pomohl Jihoafrické republice dosáhnout ohromného skóre 304/6.

Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.

F・W・ムルナウの『ノスフェラトゥ：恐怖の交響曲』は、それ自体がリメイク作品である。ブラム・ストーカーの、読み始めたら止まらなくなるような熱病的な小説『ドラキュラ』の無許可の映画化であり、ムルナウと脚本家のヘンリック・ガレーンは、原作の魅力的な要素を多く残しつつ、独自の重要な変更点も加えている。たとえば、現在では定着している「太陽光によって吸血鬼が滅びる」という設定は、ストーカーの原作にはどこにも登場しない、彼らの創作によるものである。  
私はおそらく、まだ感受性の強い年齢で『ノスフェラトゥ』を観た。6歳のとき、PBSでそのような作品が放送されており、ベビーシッターにとっては家が燃えていさえすればそれでよかったのだろう。だが、いつ観ても、私はこの作品に深く打ちのめされていたはずだ。まるで墓場から漏れる冷たい風を感じたかのようだった。（その影響は長期間にわたり、30数年後には私はこの映画とその制作過程に触発された小説を出版している。）  
この作品が与えるのは、単なる恐怖ではなく、むしろ心の奥底に忍び寄るような陰湿な不安感であり、そのすべての源はノスフェラトゥ自身という存在にある。マックス・シュレックの演技は、今から102年後である現在でも、邪悪かつ威厳を備えた忌まわしさの基準であり続けている。シュレックが演じる吸血鬼は、悪夢の中の人物やクモの巣に静かに潜むクモのように不気味な静けさを持ち、彼が住む世界もまた、時に同様に不穏な空気を漂わせる。主人公のフッターがノスフェラトゥの城で恐ろしい一夜を過ごした後、鏡に映る自分の首にかまれた痕に気づき、ほほ笑む場面がある。

src_text: When it comes to those who have waded into that kind of deep water, some have tried the Let's-really-shake-things-up solution. There's the lamentable 1962 remake of "The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari," for instance, which not only eliminated the central figure of Cesare the somnambulist but also featured a Caligari who instead of practicing diabolic hypnotism spent his time showing the heroine offensive pictures. Other filmmakers have chosen the even more baffling route of changing almost nothing, such as Gus Van Sant's nearly shot-for-shot 1998 remake of "Psycho." The number of disappointed moviegoers you risk in remaking a masterpiece from 1922 is smaller, for obvious reasons, but even so, the director Robert Eggers has made clear in any number of interviews his understanding that his new "Nosferatu" is re-engaging one of the greatest of the silent movies. (In 2016, when he was first attempting to remake the film, he told an interviewer that it felt "ugly and blasphemous and egomaniacal and disgusting" to take up that project so early into his career.)

src_text: I've always thought that one of the most insoluble aesthetic problems going is remaking a movie masterpiece. I certainly understand the impulse to passionately re-engage such a work, but if the definition of a masterwork is something peerless at what it sought to accomplish, how do you remake it without simply reiterating it? src_text: When it comes to those who have waded into that kind of deep water, some have tried the Let's-really-shake-things-up solution. There's the lamentable 1962 remake of "The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari," for instance, which not only eliminated the central figure of Cesare the somnambulist but also featured a Caligari who instead of practicing diabolic hypnotism spent his time showing the heroine offensive pictures. Other filmmakers have chosen the even more baffling route of changing almost nothing, such as Gus Van Sant's nearly shot-for-shot 1998 remake of "Psycho." The number of disappointed moviegoers you risk in remaking a masterpiece from 1922 is smaller, for obvious reasons, but even so, the director Robert Eggers has made clear in any number of interviews his understanding that his new "Nosferatu" is re-engaging one of the greatest of the silent movies. (In 2016, when he was first attempting to remake the film, he told an interviewer that it felt "ugly and blasphemous and egomaniacal and disgusting" to take up that project so early into his career.)

Fjöldi vonsvikinna kvikmyndagesta sem þú áhættir að valda með því að endurgera meistaraverk frá 1922 er vissulega minni, af augljósum ástæðum, en samt sem áður hefur leikstjórinn Robert Eggers gert ljóst í fjölmörgum viðtölum að hann skilji að „Nosferatu“-mynd hans sé endurtekning á einni af merkustu myndunum heims úr hljóðlausu kvikmyndatímabilinu. src_text: But the most destabilizing figure might well be Hutter's wife, Ellen, our heroine, who's again and again shown to be telepathically on the monster's wavelength, even when he's thousands of miles away, so that polarities like good and evil or desire and repulsion seem to just evaporate while we watch. That last aspect alone would seem to land this story in Robert Eggers's wheelhouse. Part of the subversive energy of movies like "The Witch," "The Lighthouse" and "The Northman" derives from what feels like modern takes on historical characters in thrall to dark passions so that the distantly historical is both granted its strangeness and animated by a scrutinizing modern sensibility. At its best, his version both evokes and reconceives Murnau's most brilliant visual ideas. Murnau's masterful use of the opacities of dark archways from which the vampire can emerge and into which he can dissolve is both echoed and made new. Murnau's famously arresting use of shadows to visualize the vampire's defiling reach is reimagined when those shadows in this new version extend themselves in a 360-degree pan that evokes their vertiginous inescapability. And the shadow of the vampire's hand now extends across the entire city, repurposing the most memorable image from Murnau's "Faust."

src_text: I've always thought that one of the most insoluble aesthetic problems going is remaking a movie masterpiece. I certainly understand the impulse to passionately re-engage such a work, but if the definition of a masterwork is something peerless at what it sought to accomplish, how do you remake it without simply reiterating it? There's a reason no one has tried second versions of Fellini's "8½" or Coppola's "The Godfather" or Polanski's "Chinatown." In the case of Fellini's achievement, is someone going to produce a more harrowing portrait of the self-deluding toxicity of male narcissism? In the case of Coppola's, of the corrosive effects of power? Or in the case of Polanski's, of the Hey-nothing-personal malevolence of late-model capitalism? (Water itself in that movie turns out to be the commodity that's manipulated for profit.)

src_text: South African opener Matthew Breetzke etched his name into the record books by becoming the first batter to score 150 runs on ODI debut in second match of the ongoing tri-series against New Zealand at the Gaddafi Stadium on Monday. His stunning knock of 150 off 148 balls, laced with 11 fours and five sixes, surpassed the previous record held by the legendary West Indies' batter Desmond Haynes, who scored 148 in his maiden ODI innings against Australia back in 1978. Before Breetzke's innings, the highest score on ODI debut for South Africa was 124 by Colin Ingram against Zimbabwe in 2010. Now, Breetzke stands alone at the top, delivering a performance that showcased patience, aggression, and remarkable shot selection as South Africa posted a mammoth 304/6.

src_text: I've always thought that one of the most insoluble aesthetic problems going is remaking a movie masterpiece. I certainly understand the impulse to passionately re-engage such a work, but if the definition of a masterwork is something peerless at what it sought to accomplish, how do you remake it without simply reiterating it? There's a reason no one has tried second versions of Fellini's "8½" or Coppola's "The Godfather" or Polanski's "Chinatown." In the case of Fellini's achievement, is someone going to produce a more harrowing portrait of the self-deluding toxicity of male narcissism? In the case of Coppola's, of the corrosive effects of power? Or in the case of Polanski's, of the Hey-nothing-personal malevolence of late-model capitalism? (Water itself in that movie turns out to be the commodity that's manipulated for profit.)
target_text: „Vždycky jsem se domníval, že jedním z nejneřešitelnějších estetických problémů je přetvoření filmového mistrovského díla. src_text: South African opener Matthew Breetzke etched his name into the record books by becoming the first batter to score 150 runs on ODI debut in second match of the ongoing tri-series against New Zealand at the Gaddafi Stadium on Monday. His stunning knock of 150 off 148 balls, laced with 11 fours and five sixes, surpassed the previous record held by the legendary West Indies' batter Desmond Haynes, who scored 148 in his maiden ODI innings against Australia back in 1978. Before Breetzke's innings, the highest score on ODI debut for South Africa was 124 by Colin Ingram against Zimbabwe in 2010. Now, Breetzke stands alone at the top, delivering a performance that showcased patience, aggression, and remarkable shot selection as South Africa posted a mammoth 304/6.

src_text: But the most destabilizing figure might well be Hutter's wife, Ellen, our heroine, who's again and again shown to be telepathically on the monster's wavelength, even when he's thousands of miles away, so that polarities like good and evil or desire and repulsion seem to just evaporate while we watch. That last aspect alone would seem to land this story in Robert Eggers's wheelhouse. Part of the subversive energy of movies like "The Witch," "The Lighthouse" and "The Northman" derives from what feels like modern takes on historical characters in thrall to dark passions so that the distantly historical is both granted its strangeness and animated by a scrutinizing modern sensibility. At its best, his version both evokes and reconceives Murnau's most brilliant visual ideas. Murnau's masterful use of the opacities of dark archways from which the vampire can emerge and into which he can dissolve is both echoed and made new. Murnau's famously arresting use of shadows to visualize the vampire's defiling reach is reimagined when those shadows in this new version extend themselves in a 360-degree pan that evokes their vertiginous inescapability. And the shadow of the vampire's hand now extends across the entire city, repurposing the most memorable image from Murnau's "Faust."
target_text: Nejvíce destabilizující postavou však může být Hutterova manželka Ellen, naše hrdinka, která je znovu a znovu ukázána jako telepaticky naladěná na vlnu monstra, a to i když je vzdáleno tisíce mil, takže polarity jako dobro a zlo nebo touha a odpor se zdají mizet, zatímco se na to díváme. Tento poslední aspekt by sám o sobě mohl znamenat, že se tato historie ocitne v režii Roberta Eggerse. Část subverzivní energie filmů jako „The Witch“, „The Lighthouse“ a „The Northman“ vychází z toho, co se zdá být moderním pohledem na historické postavy v zajetí temných vášní, takže vzdálená historie je jak svěřena své podivnosti, tak oživena prozkoumávající moderní citlivostí. V nejlepším případě jeho verze jak evokuje, tak znovu představuje Murnauovy nejbrilantnější vizuální nápady. Murnauovo mistrovské využití neprůhlednosti tmavých arkád, ze kterých může upír vystoupit a do kterých se může rozpustit, je jak zopakováno, tak i nově vytvořeno. Murnauovo proslulé působivé využití stínů k vizualizaci znesvěcujícího dosahu upíra je znovu představeno, když se tyto stíny v této nové verzi rozšíří do 360stupňového panoramatu, které evokuje jejich závratnou neodvratitelnost. A stín upírovy ruky se nyní rozprostírá přes celé město, což je opětovné využití nejpamátnějšího obrazu z Murnauova „Fausta“.

src_text: I've always thought that one of the most insoluble aesthetic problems going is remaking a movie masterpiece. I certainly understand the impulse to passionately re-engage such a work, but if the definition of a masterwork is something peerless at what it sought to accomplish, how do you remake it without simply reiterating it? There's a reason no one has tried second versions of Fellini's "8½" or Coppola's "The Godfather" or Polanski's "Chinatown." In the case of Fellini's achievement, is someone going to produce a more harrowing portrait of the self-deluding toxicity of male narcissism? In the case of Coppola's, of the corrosive effects of power? Or in the case of Polanski's, of the Hey-nothing-personal malevolence of late-model capitalism? (Water itself in that movie turns out to be the commodity that's manipulated for profit.)

src_text: F. W. Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.

Murnau „Nosferatu: Õudussümfoonia” on ise uusversioon – Bram Stokeri kergesti loetava palavikulise romaani „Dracula” loata adaptsioon – ning Murnau ja stsenarist Henrik Galeen säilitasid palju originaali köitvast, lisades samal ajal oma suured muudatused: näiteks on nemad vastutavad nüüdseks kivisse raiutud traditsiooni eest, et päikesevalgus võib vampiiri hävitada – mõte, mida Stokeri raamatus kusagil ei leidu. Nägin „Nosferatut” tõenäoliselt liiga kergesti mõjutatavas eas. Olin 6-aastane, PBS näitas selliseid asju ja mu lapsehoidja oli lihtsalt rõõmus, et ma maja maha ei põletanud. Aga mind oleks see iga kord maatasa teinud. See oli nagu oleksin hauast tuuletõmbust tundnud. (Selle mõju oli nii pikaajaline, et umbes 30 aastat hiljem avaldasin filmist ja selle tootmisest inspireeritud romaani.) Kogu asi polnud niivõrd hirmutav, kuivõrd salakavalalt häiriv, ja kõik see sai alguse Nosferatu enda kujust. Max Schrecki etteaste on 102 aastat hiljem endiselt pahaendelise ja väärika vastikuse etaloniks. Schrecki vampiiril on halvas unenäos oleva kuju või võrgus oleva ämbliku liikumatus ja maailm, milles ta elab, on kohati sama häiriv. Pärast meie kangelase Hutteri esimest hirmutavat ööd Nosferatu lossis märkab ta peeglist, et midagi on tal kaela hammustanud, ja ta naeratab.

src_text: I've always thought that one of the most insoluble aesthetic problems going is remaking a movie masterpiece. I certainly understand the impulse to passionately re-engage such a work, but if the definition of a masterwork is something peerless at what it sought to accomplish, how do you remake it without simply reiterating it? There's a reason no one has tried second versions of Fellini's "8½" or Coppola's "The Godfather" or Polanski's "Chinatown." In the case of Fellini's achievement, is someone going to produce a more harrowing portrait of the self-deluding toxicity of male narcissism? In the case of Coppola's, of the corrosive effects of power? Or in the case of Polanski's, of the Hey-nothing-personal malevolence of late-model capitalism? (Water itself in that movie turns out to be the commodity that's manipulated for profit.)
target_text: Я всегда думал, что одной из неразрешимых эстетических проблем будут оставаться переснятые шедевры кинематографа. Я, конечно же, понимаю желание с новым вдохновением переосмыслить такие работы, но, если определять шедевр как нечто неповторимое в области, в которой он создан, то как можно его переделать без повторения? Не просто так никто до сих пор не снял новые версии «8½» Феллини, «Крестного отца» Копполы или «Чайнатауна» Полански. Adding to this thread on my #Japanese #Okinawa #Rum exploration
Opened this OneRum bottle intending to daiquiri, but the fragrance or lack prompted me to pull out and get nosy. Smells a bit like Indian palm toddy. Uses sugar just from Ie island. Tempted to say Clairin like but no it's more spirit, vodka or sochu like - thin, smooth with a touch of heat (48%) just a late hint it's sugar distillate. Sochu, awamori sensibilities in making it for sure. (Mizuho Distillery)
1/3

src_text: I've always thought that one of the most insoluble aesthetic problems going is remaking a movie masterpiece. I certainly understand the impulse to passionately re-engage such a work, but if the definition of a masterwork is something peerless at what it sought to accomplish, how do you remake it without simply reiterating it? There's a reason no one has tried second versions of Fellini's "8½" or Coppola's "The Godfather" or Polanski's "Chinatown." In the case of Fellini's achievement, is someone going to produce a more harrowing portrait of the self-deluding toxicity of male narcissism? src_text: F. W. Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.

target_text: Film F. W. Murnaua „Nosferatu: Symfonie hrůzy“ je sám o sobě remakem – neautorizovanou adaptací románu „Dracula“, Bramovy Stokerovy posedle čtivé noční můry v podobě románu. Murnau se scenáristou Henrikem Galeenem zachovali mnoho z toho, co bylo na originále fascinující, a zároveň do něj vnesli své vlastní zásadní změny: Jsou například zodpovědní za nyní pevně zakořeněnou tradici, že sluneční světlo může upíra zničit, což je myšlenka, která se v Stokerově knize nevyskytuje. Pravděpodobně jsem „Nosferatu“ viděl v příliš raném a dojemném věku. Bylo mi šest let, PBS vysílalo takové věci a moje chůva byla prostě ráda, že jsem nezapálil dům. Ale kdykoli bych to viděl, byl bych tím zdrcen. Bylo to, jako bych ucítil chlad vycházející z hrobu. (Jeho účinky byly tak dlouhodobé, že o třicet let později jsem vydal román inspirovaný filmem a jeho produkcí.) Celé to nebylo tolik děsivé, jako spíše zákeřně znepokojující, a všechno to začalo postavou samotného Nosferata. Herecký výkon Maxe Schrecka je i po 102 letech stále měřítkem zlověstné a důstojné odpudivosti. Schreckův upír má klid postavy ze špatného snu nebo pavouka na jeho síti a svět, ve kterém žije, je někdy stejně znepokojující. Po první děsivé noci našeho hrdiny Huttera v Nosferatově hradu si všimne v zrcadle, že mu něco kouslo krk, a usměje se.

src_text: When it comes to those who have waded into that kind of deep water, some have tried the Let's-really-shake-things-up solution. There's the lamentable 1962 remake of "The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari," for instance, which not only eliminated the central figure of Cesare the somnambulist but also featured a Caligari who instead of practicing diabolic hypnotism spent his time showing the heroine offensive pictures. Other filmmakers have chosen the even more baffling route of changing almost nothing, such as Gus Van Sant's nearly shot-for-shot 1998 remake of "Psycho." The number of disappointed moviegoers you risk in remaking a masterpiece from 1922 is smaller, for obvious reasons, but even so, the director Robert Eggers has made clear in any number of interviews his understanding that his new "Nosferatu" is re-engaging one of the greatest of the silent movies. (In 2016, when he was first attempting to remake the film, he told an interviewer that it felt "ugly and blasphemous and egomaniacal and disgusting" to take up that project so early into his career.)

Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.
target_text: F. W. Murnauho film „Nosferatu: Symfonie hrůzy“ je sám o sobě remakem – neautorizovanou adaptací Stokerova kompulzivně čitelného románu „Dracula“ – a Murnau s autorem scénáře Henrikem Galeenem si ponechali mnoho z toho, co bylo na originálu strhující, a zároveň přidali své vlastní zásadní změny: Jsou zodpovědní například za dnes již pevně zakořeněnou tradici, že sluneční světlo může zničit upíra, což se ve Stokerově knize nikde neobjevuje. Film jsem pravděpodobně viděl v příliš vnímavém věku. Bylo mi šest let, PBS vysílalo takové věci a moje chůva byla prostě ráda, že jsem nebyl doma a nepodpaloval dům. Ale kdykoli jsem ho viděl, byl bych se jím nechal smetl. Bylo to jako pocit průvanu z hrobu. (Jeho účinky byly tak dlouhodobé, že jsem 30 let po jeho vzniku vydal román inspirovaný filmem a jeho výrobou.) Celá věc nebyla tak děsivá jako zákeřně znepokojující, a to vše začalo postavou samotného Nosferatu. Výkon Maxe Schrecka je 102 let po natočení filmu stále měřítkem zlověstné a důstojné odpudivosti. Schreckův upír má klid postavy ve špatném snu nebo pavouka na jeho pavučině a svět, ve kterém žije, je někdy stejně znepokojivý. Po první děsivé noci našeho hrdiny Huttera v Nosferatuově hradu si v zrcadle všimne, že mu něco kouslo krk, a usmívá se.

src_text: I've always thought that one of the most insoluble aesthetic problems going is remaking a movie masterpiece. I certainly understand the impulse to passionately re-engage such a work, but if the definition of a masterwork is something peerless at what it sought to accomplish, how do you remake it without simply reiterating it? There's a reason no one has tried second versions of Fellini's "8½" or Coppola's "The Godfather" or Polanski's "Chinatown." In the case of Fellini's achievement, is someone going to produce a more harrowing portrait of the self-deluding toxicity of male narcissism? In the case of Coppola's, of the corrosive effects of power? Or in the case of Polanski's, of the Hey-nothing-personal malevolence of late-model capitalism? (Water itself in that movie turns out to be the commodity that's manipulated for profit.)

src_text: South African opener Matthew Breetzke etched his name into the record books by becoming the first batter to score 150 runs on ODI debut in second match of the ongoing tri-series against New Zealand at the Gaddafi Stadium on Monday. His stunning knock of 150 off 148 balls, laced with 11 fours and five sixes, surpassed the previous record held by the legendary West Indies' batter Desmond Haynes, who scored 148 in his maiden ODI innings against Australia back in 1978. Before Breetzke's innings, the highest score on ODI debut for South Africa was 124 by Colin Ingram against Zimbabwe in 2010. Now, Breetzke stands alone at the top, delivering a performance that showcased patience, aggression, and remarkable shot selection as South Africa posted a mammoth 304/6.

target_text: Neben dem Senat lehnten auch Bildungsminister Mikuláš Bek und die tschechische Rektorenkonferenz die Einführung der Babysitter-Zulage ab. Murnau's masterful use of the opacities of dark archways from which the vampire can emerge and into which he can dissolve is both echoed and made new. src_text: F. W. Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.
target_text: "Nosferatu: Symfonie hrůzy" F. W. Murnaua je samo o sobě přepracováním - neoprávněnou adaptací "Draculy", Bram Stokerův nutkavě čtivý noční můra románu - a Murnau a scenárista Henrik Galeen si zachovali mnoho z toho, co bylo na originálu poutavé, a zároveň přidali své vlastní zásadní změny: Jsou například zodpovědní za nyní pevně danou tradici, že sluneční světlo může zničit upíra, což není v Stokerově knize nikde. "Nosferatu" jsem pravděpodobně viděl v příliš dojemném věku. Měl jsem 6 let, PBS takové věci ukazovala a moje chůva byla prostě ráda, že jsem nezapálil dům. Ale byl bych jím byl zasažen, kdykoli jsem ho viděl. Bylo to jako cítit průvan z hrobu. (Jeho účinky byly tak dlouhotrvající, že o 30 let později jsem publikoval román inspirovaný filmem a jeho produkcí.) Celá věc nebyla tak moc děsivá jako zákeřně znepokojivá, a to vše začalo postavou samotného Nosferatu. Max Schreckův výkon je i po 102 letech stále měřítkem pro zlověstnou a důstojnou odpornost. src_text: Proti hlídačkovnému se kromě Senátu postavili ministr školství Mikuláš Bek nebo Česká konference rektorů. Vytkli této poslanecké úpravě vládní předlohy nesystémovost, možné zneužívání a zvýšení výdajů vysokých škol, které by mohlo dosáhnout až čtvrt miliardy korun ročně. Podle dohod ministerstev školství a sociálních věcí by se příspěvek, který by podle poslanecké úpravy činil polovinu minimální mzdy, aktuálně zhruba 10.500 korun měsíčně, měl být začleněn do rodičovského příspěvku.
target_text: Neben dem Senat haben sich auch Bildungsminister Mikuláš Bek und die Tschechische Konferenz der Rektoren gegen die Betreuungspauschale ausgesprochen. Sie bemängelten an dieser parlamentarischen Änderung des Regierungsentwurfs die Nicht-Systematik, mögliche Missbrauchsmöglichkeiten und die Erhöhung der Ausgaben der Hochschulen, die bis zu einer viertel Milliarde Kronen pro Jahr erreichen könnte. Laut Absprachen der Ministerien für Bildung und Soziales sollte der Beitrag, der nach der parlamentarischen Änderung die Hälfte des Mindestlohns betragen würde, derzeit etwa 10.500 Kronen pro Monat, in den Elternbeihilfe integriert werden.

His stunning knock of 150 off 148 balls, laced with 11 fours and five sixes, surpassed the previous record held by the legendary West Indies' batter Desmond Haynes, who scored 148 in his maiden ODI innings against Australia back in 1978. Before Breetzke's innings, the highest score on ODI debut for South Africa was 124 by Colin Ingram against Zimbabwe in 2010. Now, Breetzke stands alone at the top, delivering a performance that showcased patience, aggression, and remarkable shot selection as South Africa posted a mammoth 304/6.

src_text: But the most destabilizing figure might well be Hutter's wife, Ellen, our heroine, who's again and again shown to be telepathically on the monster's wavelength, even when he's thousands of miles away, so that polarities like good and evil or desire and repulsion seem to just evaporate while we watch. That last aspect alone would seem to land this story in Robert Eggers's wheelhouse. Part of the subversive energy of movies like "The Witch," "The Lighthouse" and "The Northman" derives from what feels like modern takes on historical characters in thrall to dark passions so that the distantly historical is both granted its strangeness and animated by a scrutinizing modern sensibility. At its best, his version both evokes and reconceives Murnau's most brilliant visual ideas. Murnau's masterful use of the opacities of dark archways from which the vampire can emerge and into which he can dissolve is both echoed and made new. Murnau's famously arresting use of shadows to visualize the vampire's defiling reach is reimagined when those shadows in this new version extend themselves in a 360-degree pan that evokes their vertiginous inescapability. And the shadow of the vampire's hand now extends across the entire city, repurposing the most memorable image from Murnau's "Faust."
target_text: Ale nejvíce destabilizující postavou by mohla být Hutterova žena Ellen, naše hrdinka, která se znovu a znovu ukazuje být telepaticky naladěná na stejnou vlnu jako monstrum, dokonce i když je tisíce kilometrů daleko, takže polarity jako dobro a zlo nebo touha a odpor se před našima očima zdánlivě jednoduše rozplynou. Jen tento poslední aspekt jako by tento příběh řadil přesně do stylu Roberta Eggerse. Část podvratné energie filmů jako „Čarodějnice“, „Maják“ a „Seveřan“ pramení z něčeho, co působí jako moderní pojetí historických postav v područí temných vášní, takže dávná historie získává jak svou podivnost, tak je oživena zkoumavou moderní citlivostí. V nejlepším případě jeho verze Murnauovy nejznamenitější vizuální nápady zároveň evokuje a přetváří. Murnauovo mistrovské využití neprůhlednosti tmavých oblouků, ze kterých může upír vzejít a do kterých se může rozplynout, je jak odráženo, tak i nově vytvořeno. Murnauovo proslulé použití stínů k vizualizaci upírova znesvěceného dosahu je přepracováno tak, že se ty stíny v této nové verzi rozprostřou v 360stupňovém pohybu, který evokuje jejich závratnou nevyhnutelnost. A stín upíří ruky se nyní táhne přes celé město, čímž se znovu využívá nejpamátnější obraz z Murnauova „Fausta“.

src_text: F. W. Murnau's "Nosferatu: A Symphony of Horror" is itself a remake - an unauthorized adaptation of "Dracula," Bram Stoker's compulsively readable fever dream of a novel - and Murnau and the screenwriter Henrik Galeen retained much of what was arresting about the original while slipping in their own major changes: They're responsible, for example, for the now-set-in-stone tradition that sunlight can destroy the vampire, a notion nowhere in Stoker's book. I likely saw "Nosferatu" at too impressionable an age. I was 6, PBS was showing such things and my babysitter was simply glad I wasn't burning down the house. But I would have been flattened by it whenever I saw it. It was like having felt a draft from a grave. (Its effects were so long-lasting that 30-something years later I published a novel inspired by the film and its production.) The whole thing wasn't so much petrifying as insidiously unsettling, and all of that started with the figure of Nosferatu himself. Max Schreck's performance is, 102 years later, still the benchmark for sinister and dignified repulsiveness. Schreck's vampire has the stillness of a figure in a bad dream or a spider on its web, and the world he inhabits is at times equally disconcerting. After our hero Hutter's first frightening night in Nosferatu's castle, he notices in the mirror that something has bitten his neck, and he smiles.
target_text: „Nosferatu: Sinfónía hryllings“ eftir F. W. Murnau er sjálf endurgerð - óheimil aðlögun á „Drakúla“, þessari óstöðvandi martröð af skáldsögu eftir Bram Stoker - og Murnau og handritshöfundurinn Henrik Galeen héldu miklu af því sem var áhrifamikið í frumverkinu en bættu við sínum eigin stóru breytingum: Þeir eru til dæmis ábyrgir fyrir þeirri hefð sem nú er steypt í stein að sólarljós geti eytt vampírunni, hugmynd sem er hvergi að finna í bók Stokers. Ég sá líklega „Nosferatu“ á of áhrifagjörnum aldri. Ég var 6 ára, PBS var að sýna slíkt efni og barnfóstran var einfaldlega fegin að ég væri ekki að kveikja í húsinu. En ég hefði orðið agndofa af henni hvenær sem ég hefði séð hana. Það var eins og að finna andblæ frá gröf. (Áhrifin voru svo langvarandi að rúmum 30 árum síðar gaf ég út skáldsögu innblásna af myndinni og gerð hennar.) Heildaráhrifin voru ekki svo mikið skelfileg heldur ógnvænlega truflandi, og allt það hófst með persónu Nosferatu sjálfs. Frammistaða Max Schreck er, 102 árum síðar, enn viðmiðið fyrir óhugnanlega og virðulega viðbjóðsleika. Vampíra Schreck hefur kyrrðfígúru úr martröð eða könguló í vef sínum, og heimurinn sem hann byggir er stundum jafn truflandi. Eftir fyrstu hryllilegu nótt hetjunnar okkar Hutter í kastala Nosferatu, tekur hann eftir því í speglinum að eitthvað hefur bitið í háls hans, og hann brosir.

src_text: When it comes to those who have waded into that kind of deep water, some have tried the Let's-really-shake-things-up solution. There's the lamentable 1962 remake of "The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari," for instance, which not only eliminated the central figure of Cesare the somnambulist but also featured a Caligari who instead of practicing diabolic hypnotism spent his time showing the heroine offensive pictures. Other filmmakers have chosen the even more baffling route of changing almost nothing, such as Gus Van Sant's nearly shot-for-shot 1998 remake of "Psycho." The number of disappointed moviegoers you risk in remaking a masterpiece from 1922 is smaller, for obvious reasons, but even so, the director Robert Eggers has made clear in any number of interviews his understanding that his new "Nosferatu" is re-engaging one of the greatest of the silent movies. (In 2016, when he was first attempting to remake the film, he told an interviewer that it felt "ugly and blasphemous and egomaniacal and disgusting" to take up that project so early into his career.)
target_text: Když jde o ty, kteří se do takového hlubokého rybníka pustili, někteří zkusili řešení typu „opravdu všechno promícháme“. Například v žalostném remaku „Kabinet Dr. Caligariho“ z roku 1962 nejenže odstranili ústřední postavu Cesareho somnambulisty, ale Caligariho také namísto praktikování ďábelského hypnotismu trávil čas tím, že hrdince ukazoval urážlivé obrázky. Jiní filmaři zvolili ještě záhadnější cestu a téměř nic nezměnili, jako například Gus Van Sant v remaku „Psycha“ z roku 1998, který byl téměř kopií původního filmu. Počet zklamaných diváků, kterým hrozí při remaku mistrovského díla z roku 1922, je z pochopitelných důvodů menší, ale i tak režisér Robert Eggers v mnoha rozhovorech jasně vyjádřil své přesvědčení, že jeho nový „Nosferatu“ znovu oživuje jeden z největších němých filmů. (V roce 2016, kdy se poprvé pokoušel film znovu natočit, řekl v rozhovoru, že se mu zdálo „ošklivé, rouhačské, egomaniakální a nechutné“ se do projektu pustit tak brzy v kariéře.)

src_text: When it comes to those who have waded into that kind of deep water, some have tried the Let's-really-shake-things-up solution. There's the lamentable 1962 remake of "The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari," for instance, which not only eliminated the central figure of Cesare the somnambulist but also featured a Caligari who instead of practicing diabolic hypnotism spent his time showing the heroine offensive pictures. Other filmmakers have chosen the even more baffling route of changing almost nothing, such as Gus Van Sant's nearly shot-for-shot 1998 remake of "Psycho." The number of disappointed moviegoers you risk in remaking a masterpiece from 1922 is smaller, for obvious reasons, but even so, the director Robert Eggers has made clear in any number of interviews his understanding that his new "Nosferatu" is re-engaging one of the greatest of the silent movies. (In 2016, when he was first attempting to remake the film, he told an interviewer that it felt "ugly and blasphemous and egomaniacal and disgusting" to take up that project so early into his career.)
